transcription.tex: \textbf{Pure Mathematics Year 2}\par Chapter 4\par \textbf{Binomial Expansion}\par Negative and fractional powers · validity · approximations · partial fractions

Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. New powers}\par We extend the binomial expansion to negative and fractional powers.\[\sqrt{1+x}=(1+x)^{1/2}.\]\par The expansion is generally an infinite series, with a restricted interval of validity.
\textbf{2. A constant other than 1}\par First factor out the constant:\[(8+5x)^{-1/3}=\frac12\left(1+\frac{5x}{8}\right)^{-1/3}.\]\par Then use the binomial formula.
\textbf{3. Rational expressions}\par Partial fractions can give simpler expressions to expand:\[\frac{4-5x}{(1+x)(2-x)}.\]\par Expand each fraction, then combine like powers.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Before you start}\par For every expansion:\par 1. Identify the power and the expression replacing \(x\).\par 2. Keep brackets around negative terms.\par 3. Simplify one coefficient at a time.\par 4. State the interval of validity.\par 5. For an approximation, check that the substituted value lies in that interval.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Generalised coefficients}\[\binom nr=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}.\]\par This formula also makes sense for non-integer \(n\).\par Evaluate \(\binom{10}3,\binom{-1}2,\binom{-2}3,\binom{1/2}2\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{The binomial series}\[\begin{aligned}(1+x)^n={}&1+nx+\frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2\\&+\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3+\cdots.\end{aligned}\]\par For negative or fractional \(n\), use \(|x|<1\). For non-negative integer \(n\), the expansion terminates and is valid for every real \(x\).
Use \(n=\tfrac12\) and replace \(x\) by \(-3x\):\[1-\frac32x-\frac98x^2-\frac{27}{16}x^3+\cdots.\]\par Valid for \(|x|<\tfrac13\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Why does validity matter?}\[\frac1{1+x}=1-x+x^2-x^3+\cdots.\]\par The right side is a geometric series with ratio \(-x\).\par For which values of \(x\) does it converge?
A geometric series converges when its ratio has magnitude less than 1:\[|-x|<1\iff -1<x<1.\]

\textbf{Compare these cases}\par \(0<x<1\): signs alternate and magnitudes decrease.\par \(-1<x<0\): all terms are positive and decrease.\par \(x=1\): partial sums alternate between 1 and 0.\par \(x>1\): term magnitudes grow.\par \(x=-1\): the original fraction is undefined.\par Decreasing terms alone do not prove convergence; here the geometric-series result does.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Replace the whole expression}\par For \(\sqrt{1-3x}\), require\[|-3x|<1\iff |x|<\frac13.\]\par State the standard interval of validity for each expansion.\par (a) \((1+2x)^{-1}\)\par (b) \((1-x)^{-2}\)\par (c) \((1+x/4)^{1/2}\)\par (d) \((1-2x/3)^{-1}\)

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C4 June 2013, Q2}\par Show that, for small \(x\),\[\sqrt{\frac{1+x}{1-x}}\approx1+x+\frac12x^2.\]\par Write the expression as \((1+x)^{1/2}(1-x)^{-1/2}\).
Multiply, keeping powers up to \(x^2\):\[1+x+\left(-\frac18+\frac14+\frac38\right)x^2.\]\[\boxed{1+x+\frac12x^2}\]\par Both series are valid for \(|x|<1\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Accuracy of a truncated series}\par Approximate \(1/(1+x)\) using \(1-x+x^2\), with \(x=0.01\).

\textbf{Why is this close?}\par The first omitted term is \(-x^3=-10^{-6}\), and the later terms are smaller.\par Using more terms usually improves an approximation within the interval of convergence.\par Values near the boundary can require many more terms for comparable accuracy.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 4A, Question 5}\[f(x)=\sqrt{1+3x},\qquad -\tfrac13<x<\tfrac13.\]\par (a) Expand to \(x^3\).\par (b) Show that \(f(0.01)=\sqrt{103}/10\).\par (c) Find the percentage error in the series approximation at \(x=0.01\), to 2 significant figures.
The approximation is \(p=1.0148891875\).\par The exact value is \(v=\sqrt{1.03}\).\[\text{Percentage error}=\frac{|p-v|}{v}\times100\%.\]\par This is approximately \(0.0000031\%\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 4A, Question 6}\par In \((1+ax)^{-1/2}\), the coefficient of \(x^2\) is 24.\par (a) Find the possible values of \(a\).\par (b) Find the corresponding coefficient of \(x^3\).
\[\frac{(-1/2)(-3/2)}2a^2=\frac38a^2=24.\]\par Hence \(a^2=64\), so \(a=\pm8\).\par The cubic coefficient is \(-5a^3/16\):\par \(a=8\Rightarrow-160\); \(a=-8\Rightarrow160\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 4A, Question 8}\[h(x)=\frac6{1+5x}-\frac4{1-3x}.\]\par (a) Expand to \(x^2\). (6 marks)\par (b) Find the percentage error when the expansion estimates \(h(0.01)\), to 2 significant figures. (3 marks)\par (c) Explain why it cannot be used for \(h(0.5)\). (1 mark)
Both expansions require \(|x|<\tfrac15\).\par \(0.5\) is outside this interval.

transcription.tex: \textbf{When the constant is not 1}\par Expand \(\sqrt{4+x}\) to \(x^3\), and state the interval of validity.\par First factor out 4 inside the root:\[\sqrt{4+x}=2\left(1+\frac x4\right)^{1/2}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Check the prefactor}\par Apply the power to the factored constant as well: \(16^{-1/2}=1/4\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Avoid these common errors}\par \textbf{Signs}\par Square the whole term:\[(-3x)^2=9x^2,\qquad(-3x)^3=-27x^3.\]\par \textbf{Factorials}\par The cubic coefficient uses \(3!=6\), not 3.

\textbf{Brackets}\par In \((1-3x)^n\), every power applies to \(-3x\).\par \textbf{Constant factor}\par In \((a+bx)^n\), first write\[a^n\left(1+\frac{bx}{a}\right)^n.\]\par \textbf{Validity}\par Test \(|bx/a|<1\), not just \(|x|<1\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 4B, Question 4}\par The first three terms are\[\frac1{\sqrt{a+bx}}=3+\frac13x+\frac1{18}x^2+\cdots.\]\par (a) Find \(a\) and \(b\).\par (b) Find the coefficient of \(x^3\).
\[\frac1{\sqrt{a+bx}}=a^{-1/2}\left(1+\frac ba x\right)^{-1/2}.\]\par Constant term: \(a^{-1/2}=3\Rightarrow a=1/9\).\par Linear coefficient: \(-b/(2a^{3/2})=1/3\).\[\boxed{b=-\frac2{81}}.\]
The expansion is \(3(1-2x/9)^{-1/2}\).\par Its cubic coefficient is\[3\left(-\frac5{16}\right)\left(-\frac29\right)^3=\boxed{\frac5{486}}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 4B, Question 5}\[f(x)=\frac{3+2x-x^2}{4-x}.\]\par Prove that, for sufficiently small \(x\),\[f(x)\approx\frac34+\frac{11}{16}x-\frac5{64}x^2.\]

\[\frac1{4-x}=\frac14\left(1-\frac x4\right)^{-1}=\frac14+\frac x{16}+\frac{x^2}{64}+\cdots.\]\par Multiply by \(3+2x-x^2\).\par Constant: \(3/4\).\par Linear: \(3/16+2/4=11/16\).\par Quadratic: \(3/64+2/16-1/4=-5/64\).\[\boxed{f(x)\approx\frac34+\frac{11}{16}x-\frac5{64}x^2}.\]\par The series is valid for \(|x|<4\).
